items.title: EMCrit 437 — Massive Lithium Overdose
items.summary: The tox case that looks stable for hours and then isn't, worked through by the people who dialyse it.
items.note: Lithium is the overdose where the serum level and the patient disagree, and the decision that matters — when to call the nephrologist rather than keep observing — belongs to whoever is holding the resus phone. Weingart's format puts the dialysis threshold and the redistribution trap in the same half hour. Highest-weight source on his list, and the newest thing on it.

items.title: Are we ready for war? The clinical challenges of modern conflict
items.summary: Carley on what drone-era wounding patterns do to the trauma care he was trained to give.
items.note: Simon Carley argues the injury patterns of modern conflict — blast, prolonged field care, delayed evacuation — break the assumptions baked into civilian major trauma pathways. Part 1 is the clinical half; the promised Part 2 turns to what it means for EDs and hospitals. St Emlyn's appraisal has the UK/ANZ case mix closest to his own, which is why this lands differently than an American trauma blog would.

items.title: Who do you trust? AI in medical education
items.summary: Beardsell on the question a registrar actually faces: when is the model's answer good enough to teach from?
items.note: Written from EMCON in Mumbai, this is about trust calibration rather than AI boosterism — how a trainee should weight a model's output against a guideline, a consultant and the primary paper. It sits directly on the seam between the two things this feed keeps bringing him: critical appraisal and capable models. Worth reading alongside the Anthropic drug-development post in today's edition.

items.title: Bringing the emergency department into your lounge room
items.summary: An inside account of the Victorian Virtual ED and what it is actually diverting away from his triage desk.
items.note: The VVED now takes self-referrals, Ambulance Victoria handovers and aged-care calls, triages them virtually and sends only some of them on to a physical ED — which makes it one of the few structural changes to Victorian emergency demand that a registrar will feel in the waiting room rather than read about in a budget. The authors are candid that the hard parts were leadership and priority-setting, not the video link. System-side reading, not clinical.

items.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
items.summary: Six drug developers report what a model actually shortened — and most of it was paperwork, not chemistry.
items.note: The headline numbers are biology (a CAR-T construct 70% shorter, ~35,000 antibody designs in a month), but the most telling result is Enveda cutting manufacturing document review from 25 hours to under three. That is the same category of work that eats a hospital's accreditation and audit time. First-party and specific, with the caveat stated in the post itself: the remaining bottlenecks are regulatory and operational.

items.title: Surprise Chef :: Frogs In A Pond
items.summary: A proper write-up of the fifth Surprise Chef record, from the band that made this sound a Melbourne export.
items.note: Surprise Chef are a Melbourne instrumental soul group who landed on Big Crown — the shelf next to Menahan Street Band, Thee Sacred Souls and the Daptone records already in his collection — and have now moved to Concord Jazz for this one. Aquarium Drunkard reads it as beauty found in the uneasy marriage of the sinister and the seductive, which is a long way from a release-date blurb. The album coverage he has had so far was announcement and tour news; this is the listening.

items.title: Film Photography Mistakes: Shooting & Developing Issues, Fixed
items.summary: A diagnostic chart for ruined rolls — read the fault on the negative, then name its cause.
items.note: Taylor Blanchard works backwards from what the frame looks like to what went wrong at the camera, which is the useful direction. The 120 section is the part worth keeping: winding a roll tight enough on the take-up spool, and taping the paper leader if it slips, is exactly the failure that spoils medium-format frames. Pairs with the Plaubel Makina 67 piece he read earlier this week.

items.title: Goodbye Summer
items.summary: An honest verdict on Rollei CR200 — warm, muted, and unkind to skin.
items.note: Slide film gets written about reverentially, so a user report that says plainly where the stock fails is more useful than another appreciation. Shot on a Contax RTS II in Epping Forest, which makes it a fair test of the emulsion in flat autumn light rather than in ideal sun. Read it as a reason to keep CR200 off portrait rolls.

items.title: Bleu de Chauffe Renders its Germinal Chore Jacket in Japanese Denim
items.summary: The French workwear house puts its chore jacket in 12oz Japanese denim — cloth change, same pattern.
items.note: The Germinal is Bleu de Chauffe's version of the bleu de travail, and seeing it cut in 12oz Japanese Stone Bio denim rather than the usual moleskin or canvas is a clean case study in how much the cloth does and how little the pattern needs to. Made in France at $342. He has read Heddels on Bleu de Chauffe's FW26 bags and denim already; this is the single garment.

items.title: Autumn/Winter highlights: En Passant, Cutler, P Johnson
items.summary: The En Passant Readers Jacket in olive moleskin — a hunting jacket with the fuss taken out.
items.note: Crompton's pick here is a simplified hunting jacket made in Portugal, and his recommendation is a cloth one: olive moleskin over everything else offered. That is the rustic-menswear argument in miniature, and it is the same reasoning that makes vintage Woolrich and Pendleton worth owning. Skip the P Johnson tailoring section; the jacket and the water-resistant Speciale coat are the parts that apply.

items.title: Dune Awakening's free Blood and Ice expansion lands December 1
items.summary: A dated, free survival expansion — cold management, ice harvesting — plus the offline mode arriving in November.
items.note: Funcom is sending players to the Polar Sink, swapping Arrakis' heat survival for extreme cold and ice harvesting, and it is free rather than paid DLC. The buried detail is the single-player offline option arriving in November, which turns an always-online survival MMO into something closer to how he plays Enshrouded and Dragonwilds. Massively OP remains the only outlet that covers survival-game patch cycles properly.

items.title: Live Nation Is Bringing a 5000-Capacity Venue to Arden Central
items.summary: A purpose-built mid-size room going up 1.5km from the CBD, in the gap between the Croxton and Rod Laver.
items.note: Melbourne is thin on rooms between 1,000 and 10,000 capacity, which is why touring acts skip the city or oversell into arenas; Live Nation is building this one at Arden Central with Populous and plans 100-plus events a year. North Melbourne, one Arden Station stop from the northside. Stage one is pencilled for 2033, so this is a long-horizon item rather than a ticket to buy.
